hook: Kick a net through the gravel of a clean mountain stream and you will find dozens of mayfly and stonefly larvae. Do the same just below a drainage pipe and you may find almost none, only midges and worms. You did not need a chemistry kit. The insects told you the water was polluted.

prereq.q: Which organisms live in a coral's tissues and make food by photosynthesis?
prereq.why: Algae inside the coral make food by photosynthesis and share it with the coral.

prereq.q: What happens to an organism in its zone of physiological stress?
options: It survives but is stressed and may not reproduce
prereq.why: Outside its optimal range, an organism is stressed and does worse.

figure.caption: Stream insects sorted by how much pollution they tolerate: sensitive species disappear first, tolerant ones take over.

chain.cause: People add pollutants, heat, sediment, oil or plastic to water
chain.effect: conditions move outside the tolerance range of sensitive species

chain.cause: Sensitive species die or leave, and tolerant species remain or increase
chain.effect: the community changes, which indicator species reveal

chain.cause: On reefs, heat stress makes corals expel their algae
chain.effect: corals bleach, starve and may die, and reef species lose habitat

chain.cause: Oil coats animals and plastics are eaten
chain.effect: animals lose insulation, are poisoned, or starve with full stomachs

ideas: Species differ in their range of tolerance. Indicator species such as mayfly, stonefly and caddisfly larvae disappear when water quality falls; midges and worms tolerate pollution.
Coral bleaching: heat stress (and pollution) makes corals expel their algae, so they turn white and may starve. Sediment blocks light and smothers reefs.
Oil spills coat feathers and fur, poison animals and smother shorelines. Cleanup uses booms, skimmers and, with care, dispersants.
Ocean plastics entangle animals and are eaten; they break into microplastics that enter food webs and carry toxic chemicals.

misconception.wrong: A bleached coral has been bleached by chemicals in the water.
misconception.right: Bleaching means the coral has expelled its algae, usually because of heat stress. The white is the coral's skeleton showing through clear tissue.

summary: Pollution changes ecosystems by pushing conditions outside species' tolerance ranges. Indicator species such as mayfly larvae reveal water quality. Heat stress bleaches corals by making them expel their algae; sediment smothers reefs; oil spills coat and poison wildlife; and plastics entangle animals and break into microplastics that enter food webs.
